interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: RoughNet: Mapping Arctic Sea Ice Roughness Using Diffusion-Based Super-Resolution of Satellite Imagery
papers.authors: Tessa Cannon , Michel Tsamados , Petru Manescu , Thomas Newman , Christian Haas , Veit Helm , Weibin Chen , Randall Scharien
papers.abstract: Accurate estimation of landfast sea ice roughness is critical for climate modeling and safe Arctic over-ice travel, yet existing approaches rely on costly airborne surveys or sparse in-situ measurements, limiting spatial coverage and operational scalability. Here we show that high-resolution sea ice topography can be reconstructed directly from optical satellite imagery using a conditional diffusion framework. Our approach, RoughNet, learns to map 10 m Sentinel-2 multispectral images to locally normalized 1 m surface elevation residual fields, enabling fine-scale roughness characterization from widely available satellite data. Trained on airborne LiDAR data from two Arctic regions and evaluated on an unseen third Arctic region, the model generalizes across diverse ice conditions and partially reproduces small-scale topographic structure. The best-performing model achieves an out-of-domain root mean squared error of 9 cm while preserving the statistical and spectral properties of the underlying roughness field. These results demonstrate that generative diffusion models can recover physically meaningful surface structure from optical imagery alone, providing a scalable pathway for high-resolution sea ice mapping and roughness estimation in data-sparse environments.
papers.Reasons for match: Diffusion-based super-resolution for sea ice roughness from satellite imagery, directly relevant to astronomical image analysis and generative models for science.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem of estimating sea ice roughness from optical satellite imagery, which is critical for climate modeling but traditionally requires costly airborne surveys. The main AI idea is a conditional diffusion framework (RoughNet) that learns to map 10 m Sentinel-2 images to 1 m surface elevation residuals, trained on LiDAR data and generalizing to unseen regions. This matters for astronomy because diffusion models are increasingly used for image super-resolution, denoising, and inpainting in JWST and other survey data. An astronomer could imagine using a similar conditional diffusion approach to enhance resolution of astronomical images (e.g., from JWST or HST) or to reconstruct fine-scale structure from lower-resolution data. A limitation is that the model requires paired high-resolution training data (e.g., LiDAR), which may not be available for astronomical targets, and the out-of-domain generalization may not hold for very different data distributions.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the conditional diffusion architecture details and how the model handles multi-spectral input.
Check the out-of-domain generalization results on the unseen third Arctic region for evidence of robustness.
Examine the statistical and spectral property preservation metrics to assess physical fidelity.

papers.title: Attention-Free and Lightweight Token Reduction for Efficient Vision-Language Models
papers.authors: Xuanyi Hao , Zuoyuan Zhang , Zhibo Wang , Xiaoyi Pang , Jiahui Hu , Jiacheng Du , Shuguo Zhuo
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in multimodal understanding, yet remain challenging to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices due to the substantial computational overhead of processing numerous visual tokens. Token reduction is a promising direction for accelerating VLMs inference, but existing approaches either rely on attention maps that are incompatible with modern acceleration frameworks or depend on computationally intensive pairwise similarity comparisons, which undermine scalability and negate their practical benefits in deployment. In this paper, we propose an attention-free and lightweight token reduction framework as a plug-and-play module for VLMs, which preserves both important and diverse tokens to produce a compact visual representation. First, to enable attention-free importance estimation, we adopt an information-theoretic perspective and quantify token information using a novel entropy-based criterion, retaining those with more expressive and less degenerate feature representations. Second, to ensure diverse visual coverage in a lightweight manner, we introduce a transformation-induced consistency signal where similar tokens yield similar signals, such that sorting by this signal places similar tokens close to each other and enables stride-based selection to produce a diverse token set. Extensive experiments across multiple VLMs benchmarks demonstrate that our framework achieves a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off, maintaining competitive performance under aggressive compression.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses token reduction for Vision-Language Models, which is relevant for efficient processing of JWST images and multimodal astronomical data on resource-constrained systems.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of reducing the computational cost of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by cutting down the number of visual tokens processed. The authors propose a lightweight, attention-free framework that uses an entropy-based criterion to keep informative tokens and a transformation-induced consistency signal to ensure diverse visual coverage, all without relying on computationally expensive attention maps. For astronomy, this could enable running multimodal models (e.g., combining JWST images with spectral or catalog data) on modest hardware, making large-scale survey analysis more accessible. A concrete workflow would be feeding cutouts of high-redshift galaxies or little red dots into a VLM for classification or description, with the token reduction module accelerating inference. A key caveat is that the method is tested on standard VLM benchmarks, not astronomical data, so its performance on noisy, sparse, or high-dynamic-range astronomical images needs verification.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the entropy-based importance estimation is robust to astronomical image characteristics like high dynamic range and sparse sources.
Look for ablation studies showing the trade-off between compression ratio and accuracy on fine-grained classification tasks relevant to astronomy.
Verify whether the method requires any fine-tuning on the target domain or works as a true plug-and-play module.

papers.title: From Surface Forecasting to Observability Forecasting: A Latent World Model for Cloud-Aware EO Monitoring
papers.abstract: The bottleneck of Earth Observation processing chains is not the arrival of new imagery but whether the surface is actually visible when the image arrives. We study this as an observability forecasting problem on EarthNet2021. Given recent multispectral imagery and exogenous weather drivers, the goal is to predict whether the next acquisition will be usable and, if not, when a usable view is likely to return. To do this, we adapt LeWorldModel, a joint-embedding predictive architecture world model, to cloud-aware Earth Observation sequences. The final pipeline converts raw minicubes into episodic HDF5 sequences with five image channels (blue, green, red, near-infrared, cloud mask) and eight meteorological and calendar covariates. The resulting model has 18.0M trainable parameters and is trained from scratch on 23,904 training episodes. The trained leWorldModel is evaluated under a locked protocol: linear probes are fit on train only, calibration choices are set on an internal validation split, and the fitted heads are then frozen for valsplit, IID, OOD, and extreme evaluation. On the full frozen-bundle observability benchmark, LeWorldModel consistently outperforms persistence. For next-step usability, balanced accuracy ranges from 0.769 to 0.887, compared with 0.493 to 0.556 for persistence. For exact first-usable-horizon prediction, accuracy ranges from 0.602 to 0.806, compared with 0.120 to 0.369 for persistence. Against a frozen LightGBM baseline fit on the same training windows, LeWorldModel is better on continuous clear/cloud regression and on exact recovery timing on valsplit, IID, and extreme, while LightGBM is stronger on the simpler binary any-usable-within-six task and is more robust on OOD. In separate sampled diagnostic analyses, LeWM also produces strong ranking-based anomaly signals under synthetic temporal inconsistencies.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses cloud-aware Earth observation forecasting using a latent world model; highly relevant to astronomical survey scheduling and observability prediction.
papers.Short digest: Can a world model predict when Earth observation images will be usable despite clouds? The paper adapts LeWorldModel, a joint-embedding predictive architecture, to forecast cloud-free visibility. For astronomy, this directly transfers to predicting observing conditions (e.g., weather, seeing, moon phase) for ground-based telescopes or scheduling JWST observations. A limitation is that the model is trained on EarthNet2021 (satellite imagery), not astronomical data, so retraining on astronomical weather/observability data would be needed.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the specific architecture details of LeWorldModel and how it handles temporal sequences.
Check whether the model outputs uncertainty estimates for its predictions.
Assess the computational requirements for training and inference on astronomical timeseries data.
Look for ablation studies showing the importance of each input channel (meteorological, calendar, etc.).

papers.title: A novel unsupervised machine learning strategy to handle multimodal cardiac PET/MRI data
papers.authors: Brunnhilde Ponsi (1 and 2), Thomas Carlier (1 and 2), Lara Marteau (1 and 3), Aurélien Monnet (4), Thomas Eugène (1 and 2), Jean-Michel Serfaty (1 and 5), Nicolas Piriou (1 and 3), Hatem Necib (1 and 2) ((1) Nantes Université, CHU Nantes, Nantes, France, (2) CRCI2NA, INSERM UMR 1307, Nantes, France, (3) Cardiology Department, INSERM UMR 1307, CIC 1413, l'institut du Thorax, Nantes, France, (4) Siemens Healthineers France, Courbevoie, France, (5) Radiology Department, l'institut du Thorax, Nantes, France)
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Medical Physics (physics.med-ph)
papers.abstract: Arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy is a genetic myocardial disease difficult to diagnose due to the lack of gold standard criteria. Simultaneous PET/MR imaging, combined with multiparametric quantitative analysis, could facilitate the identification of different profiles related to the phenotype and progression of cardiomyopathy. This preliminary study focuses on a methodological strategy for dealing with PET/MRI data, including inter-patient data linkage and regional analysis. Two-step clustering was applied to T1 and T2 maps, LGE, and 18F-FDG-PET images of 99 patients genetically diagnosed with arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy. Each patient's images were independently z-scored and summed into a single volume, which was clustered into supervoxels. Thirty-two inter-patient groups of supervoxels were obtained by spectral clustering. An "abnormality" score was assigned to each cluster and modality, and used to visualise abnormal regions likely associated with disease. They enabled the generation of automated textual and bullseye health reports for each patient, which were compared with cardiac imager assessments using balanced accuracy in repeated nested cross-validation. This approach was further validated on a larger cohort of 167 numerical phantoms. The reports generated by clustering accurately identified most of the cardiac physicians' observations (BA = 0.76 $\pm$ 0.04 in repeated nested cross-validation on patients, and BA $\ge$ 0.8 on phantoms). Furthermore, the identified abnormal clusters closely matched their visual observations, facilitating the identification of varying degrees of fibrosis or inflammation on the images. This approach enables a more systematic handling of multimodal PET/MRI data to characterise myocardial heterogeneity in arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy patients.
papers.Reasons for match: Paper directly addresses multimodal data fusion (PET/MRI) with unsupervised clustering, which maps onto astronomical source classification and SED fitting with multi-wavelength data.
papers.Short digest: This paper develops an unsupervised machine learning strategy to handle multimodal cardiac PET/MRI data for diagnosing arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy. It applies two-step clustering: first, each patient's images are z-scored and summed into a single volume, then clustered into supervoxels; second, spectral clustering groups these supervoxels across patients into 32 inter-patient groups. An abnormality score is assigned to each cluster and modality, enabling automated health reports. For astronomy, this approach is directly transferable: instead of PET/MRI, one could use JWST NIRCam and MIRI images, or multi-wavelength catalogs. The two-step clustering could identify distinct galaxy populations (e.g., little red dots, quiescent galaxies, AGN) without labels. A concrete workflow would be applying this to a multi-band JWST survey to find anomalous sources or to perform unsupervised SED-based classification. A limitation is that the method assumes all images are co-registered and have the same spatial resolution, which may not hold for multi-instrument astronomical data.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check how the z-scoring and supervoxel clustering handle different noise levels and PSF sizes across modalities.
Look for the spectral clustering parameters and whether they are robust to different numbers of sources.
Examine the abnormality score definition and whether it can separate different physical classes (e.g., AGN vs. star formation).

papers.title: PlumeQuant: Uncertainty-aware consistency assessment of methane plume masks and emission-rate estimates
papers.authors: Parisa Masnadi Khiabani , Wolfgang Jentner , Alireza Rangrazjeddi , Michael C. Wimberly , Binbin Weng , David Ebert , Charles Nicholson
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Instrumentation and Methods for Astrophysics (astro-ph.IM)
papers.abstract: Imaging spectrometers increasingly distribute source-resolved methane plume products in which the plume mask, integrated mass enhancement (IME), plume length, emission rate, and uncertainty are physically and algorithmically linked. Using 63 EMIT-derived Carbon Mapper plume records from 27 scenes, we show that these published scalar quantities do not uniquely constrain the plume boundary: substantially different yet plausible masks reproduce the same IME, plume length, and emission rate. Genetic-algorithm (GA) ensembles conditioned on the published IME and plume length make this equifinality explicit: the high-confidence core selected by nearly all target-consistent masks covers a median of 13% of the plausible footprint envelope, and ambiguity is largest for weak, low-overlap plumes. The diagnostics come from PlumeQuant, which recomputes IME, plume length, emission rate, and five-term uncertainty from distributed product components under stated conventions and evaluates four mask representations: the distributed reference mask, a transparent Carbon Mapper-informed analogue (CM-like), the GA ensemble, and optional expert edits. The CM-like mask is generated per plume without access to the reference mask or published quantities, with settings fixed once on a scene-disjoint 44-plume development split. It reproduced published IME with +0.72% median difference and emission rate with +0.16% (6.98% mean absolute), reached 0.843 median intersection-over-union against the reference masks, and matched the published uncertainty scale (median ratio 1.01). Holdout mean absolute errors were 7.6% (IME), 9.5% (length), and 6.1% (rate). These are product-level consistency diagnostics, not independent validation. They flag weak, offset, or ambiguous plumes for expert review.
papers.Reasons for match: Paper directly addresses uncertainty quantification and consistency assessment for methane plume masks from imaging spectrometers, which maps onto similar challenges for astronomical source detection and flux measurement.
papers.Short digest: This paper presents PlumeQuant, a framework for assessing the consistency and uncertainty of methane plume masks and emission-rate estimates from imaging spectrometers like EMIT. It uses genetic algorithm ensembles to show that different plausible masks can reproduce the same published integrated mass enhancement and plume length, revealing equifinality. The high-confidence core covers only a median of 13% of the plausible footprint envelope. For astronomy, this is directly relevant: similar equifinality issues arise in source deblending, SED fitting, and morphological classification. A concrete workflow would be applying PlumeQuant's ensemble approach to JWST source masks to understand how much the mask boundary affects derived fluxes and colors. A limitation is that the method is designed for methane plumes with specific physical properties (e.g., Gaussian-like concentration profiles), which may not directly transfer to astronomical sources with different spatial distributions.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the genetic algorithm details: how are masks parameterized and what constraints are used?
Check the uncertainty propagation from mask to emission-rate estimate.
Examine the diagnostics for weak, offset, or ambiguous plumes and whether they have analogs for astronomical sources.
